title: MPMA: Preference Manipulation Attack Against Model Context Protocol
pdf_path: papers/MPMA_Preference Manipulation Attack Against Model Context Protocol.pdf
threat_model_summary: A malicious MCP server manipulates its tool name and description so that the host agent prefers it over competing tools. The attack is semantic advertising at the tool-selection layer, not a protocol or code exploit; the adversary controls only its own published metadata and does not modify the host or other servers.
core_contributions: MPMA: a preference manipulation attack on MCP tool selection
Direct preference manipulation through tool name/description variants
A genetic-algorithm variant that evolves descriptions to maximize selection
Measurement across five models, showing mean attack success from 22.19% (GPT-4o) to 91.88% (Gemini)
Stealthiness evaluation with an LLM judge and human ratings
limitations: The paper outsources related work, prompts, dataset, GA comparison, and economic analysis to a full arXiv version absent from the PDF
No defense is proposed or evaluated
Algorithm 1 pool initialization is self-contradictory
The claim that Au is consistently best conflicts with GPT-4o where Su exceeds Au and Ex falls below baseline
Success rate is 100% for all models and the preference label is post hoc, making SR close to tautological
TPR formula and human aggregation are undefined; Figure 5 uses different reference lines for LLM and human panels
Figure 1 places the base LLM outside the MCP host, contradicting Section 2.1
Baseline assumes identical competitors while Section 5 says competitor descriptions are rewritten
Ten queries per server, single run, no confidence intervals, seeds, or temperature; no multiple-comparison correction
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no cryptographic definition, game, construction, theorem, proof, or reduction
applied_crypto_links: None; no signing, attestation, OAuth, TLS, or registry verification is used
Signed tool descriptions would authenticate publisher identity and content integrity, not the preference semantics of the description
evidence_refs: pp.1-7 threat model, MPMA, experiments, and discussion
p.8 acknowledgments/references start; p.9 references browsed only

title: Shadows in the Code: Exploring the Risks and Defenses of LLM-based Multi-Agent Software Development Systems
pdf_path: papers/Shadows in the Code_Exploring the Risks and Defenses of LLM-based Multi-Agent Software Development Systems.pdf
threat_model_summary: A malicious agent participates in a multi-agent software development pipeline (ChatDev, MetaGPT, AgentVerse) and injects instructions into inter-agent messages to make the system generate malicious code. The adversary controls one agent's messages, not the framework or model weights; the defense is a prompt-level self-check.
core_contributions: Two attack modes, MU-BA and BU-MA, against multi-agent software development
Evaluation across ChatDev, MetaGPT, and AgentVerse on 480 tasks and 12 malicious behaviors
ASR up to 93% (MU-BA) and 84% (BU-MA) depending on framework
Adv-IMBIA prompt-level defense that reduces ASR in several settings
Comparison across 13 backbone models
limitations: No independent limitations or ethics section; no appendix
Defense is prompt-based self-checking with five undisclosed criteria
No adaptive attack against the defense
No benign utility or defense-cost measurement
ASR is judged by GPT-4o with no judge validation
Figure 3 shows quality degradation under attack that conflicts with the no-significant-degradation claim
RQ1/RQ2 text conflicts with Figures 6-7 for AgentVerse
The claim that defending only the critical stage approximates full defense holds only for MetaGPT
ASR reductions are reported as percentages but are percentage points
The ablation claim that Td contributes more than Ci fails for BU-MA
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no cryptographic primitive, definition, theorem, proof, or reduction
applied_crypto_links: None; no signing, SBOM, attestation, or sandbox is evaluated
Signed code or SBOM would bind origin and build, not the semantic safety of generated code
evidence_refs: pp.1-7 attacks, defense, experiments, and analysis
p.8 acknowledgments/references start; p.9 references browsed only

title: Attack the Messages, Not the Agents: A Multi-round Adaptive Stealthy Tampering Framework for LLM-MAS
pdf_path: papers/Attack the Messages, Not the Agents_A Multi-round Adaptive Stealthy Tampering Framework for LLM-MAS.pdf
threat_model_summary: A man-in-the-middle attacker controls part of the communication links in an LLM multi-agent system, intercepting, modifying, and forwarding inter-agent messages over multiple rounds. The attacker cannot directly change agent state or model weights; messages are assumed to lack authentication and integrity protection.
core_contributions: MAST: a multi-round adaptive stealthy message-tampering framework for LLM-MAS
MCTS-based planning plus DPO training for tampering policy optimization
Evaluation on flat, chain, and hierarchical topologies and multiple tasks
ASR up to 95.3 with stealthiness up to 82.6
Ablations separating tampering reward, preference detection, semantic embedding, and exploration
limitations: The attack assumes unauthenticated, integrity-unprotected inter-agent channels and never evaluates signatures, MACs, TLS, nonces, or replay protection
Stealthiness is measured by a single Llama-3.1-70B semantic detector with no FPR/FNR or post-detection action
Attack training relies on a simulatable LLM-MAS, a GPT-4o process reward model, and known tasks/topologies
Embedding functions are unnamed; no learning rate, hardware, seeds, or code/artifact
Single run without variance
Table 1 bold/underline annotations are inconsistent
Table 2 defines PD as tau while the text calls it pairwise preference detection; removing SE raises ASR in MAB
Figure 4(b) claims greater epsilon sensitivity while delta varies more
Notation overload: A denotes both the agent set and the system; G denotes both graph and task
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no cryptographic definition, game, construction, theorem, proof, or reduction
The MITM setting is a cryptographic threat model in name only; no MAC/signature forgery or advantage is modeled
applied_crypto_links: None; no TLS, mTLS, signatures, MAC/HMAC, nonces, replay windows, or key management are used or evaluated
Message-level signatures plus monotonic nonces would block link-only tampering under this threat model, but not a compromised sender or leaked key
evidence_refs: pp.1-7 threat model, MAST, experiments, and discussion
p.8 acknowledgments/references start; p.9 references browsed only

title: Make Agent Defeat Agent: Automatic Detection of Taint-Style Vulnerabilities in LLM-based Agents
pdf_path: papers/Make Agent Defeat Agent_Automatic Detection of Taint-Style Vulnerabilities in LLM-based Agents.pdf
threat_model_summary: Untrusted inputs from external sources flow through an LLM agent's tool invocations into sensitive sinks, producing taint-style vulnerabilities. The tool performs automated gray-box fuzzing and concolic execution over agent source code; there is no cryptographic adversary.
core_contributions: An automated taint-style vulnerability detector for LLM-based agents
Directed gray-box fuzzing plus concolic execution to reach sink callsites
Evaluation on 20 open-source agents and 828 sink callsites
34 zero-days, 100% precision on manual review, and 97.14% recall on 35 ground-truth bugs
23 CVEs assigned, with 69.01 CPU hours and 121.78 minutes average time-to-exploit
limitations: Single prompt only; second-order vulnerabilities such as Devika are not covered
Complex sanitizers sampled at 4.82% may cause false negatives
Ground truth is aggregated from two tools; the 35th case's provenance is unexplained
100% precision is author manual review with no independent labeling or confidence intervals
Manual sink lists and instrumentation; Python source only; GPT-4o only
Only Web-service agents; comparison limited to LLMSmith
The paper reports both 23 and 27 CVEs
69.01 CPU hours is close to the 828 times 5-minute budget, in tension with early break on PoC
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no cryptographic primitive, definition, theorem, proof, or reduction
Taint-style vulnerability is a program-analysis property, not a cryptographic one
applied_crypto_links: None; CodeQL, Z3, and py-conbyte are program analysis, not cryptographic engineering
No signatures, attestation, or secure compilation are evaluated
evidence_refs: pp.1-15 design, implementation, evaluation, and limitations
pp.20-21 appendices A-C; pp.16-19 references browsed only

title: MUZZLE: Adaptive Agentic Red-Teaming of Web Agents Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks
pdf_path: papers/MUZZLE_Adaptive Agentic Red-Teaming of Web Agents Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks.pdf
threat_model_summary: A black-box attacker with user-level access observes local agent-LLM traffic and injects malicious content into web applications, adapting payloads across rounds based on victim behavior. The attacker cannot modify the server, scaffold, or training; the evaluation is not adaptive to defenses.
core_contributions: MUZZLE: an adaptive agentic red-teaming framework for web-agent IPI
Trajectory-driven vessel ranking, context-aware payload generation, and judge-based failure attribution
Evaluation across 4 applications, 3 LLMs, and 2 scaffolds with 44 end-to-end runs
ASR 86.7% versus 20.0% for WASP
Post-hoc evaluation of 9 prompt-level detectors, with best TPR 32.2% at 5.5% FPR
limitations: 44 is the number of end-to-end runs, not 44 distinct attacks, conflicting with abstract wording
Three cross-application attacks cover only two targets and three runs
Section 4.1 says three user tasks but describes a fourth Northwind task
Webhook text says all five runs partial while tables report four
Qwen3-32B in Table 3 vs Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct in text
Table 9 mislabels LlamaGuard 2 as Llama PromptGuard 2
Abstract lists privacy where the evaluation concerns integrity
Table 6 selects only targets with confirmed E2E success, ten runs per app
Table 5 percentages sum to about 101.9%
Single environment, k=5, no confidence intervals, no system or cryptographic defense evaluation
Adaptive only to victim behavior, not to defenses
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no cryptographic primitive, definition, game, theorem, proof, or reduction
Assertions are cURL application-state checks, not attestation
applied_crypto_links: None; no content provenance signatures, isolation, capability tokens, or attestation are evaluated
Signed content provenance would authenticate the source of page content, not whether its instructions are safe
evidence_refs: pp.1-15 framework, experiments, discussion, and ethics
pp.19-21 appendices A.1/A.2/B; pp.16-19 references browsed only
